title: Oruc Reis Surveys Signal Cyprus Pipeline Push, State Dept Says F-35 Conditions Unmet, DW Reporter Freed With Travel Ban
subhead: Turkey issued a navtex for seismic surveys on a gas pipeline route to northern Cyprus, the US confirmed Ankara still fails to meet F-35 requirements, and Deutsche Welle correspondent Alican Uludag was released under judicial control after 25 hours in custody — while Houthi strikes on Saudi tankers and a US-Saudi nuclear pact reshape the energy landscape around Turkey.

sections.heading: Oruc Reis Deploys for Cyprus Pipeline Surveys
sections.body:
Turkey issued a navigational warning (navtex) on Wednesday announcing that the seismic research vessel Oruc Reis will conduct surveys along the planned route of a natural gas pipeline from Anamur, in Mersin province, to the Teknecik power station outside Kyrenia in northern Cyprus. The surveys are scheduled to run through August 30, according to Cyprus Mail.

The pipeline project — formalized through a memorandum of understanding signed July 10 between Ankara and the Turkish Cypriot authorities — envisions two parallel 56cm-diameter pipelines stretching 101km (97km under the Levantine Sea), allowing bidirectional gas flow. Turkish Vice President Cevdet Yilmaz called it a 'historic turning point' in cooperation. Turkish Cypriot 'prime minister' Unal Ustel said the project was 'for future generations.' Turkish Energy Minister Alparslan Bayraktar confirmed the pipeline would connect to existing infrastructure linking Mersin and Alanya.

The timing has raised eyebrows in Athens and Nicosia: the Oruc Reis departed Silifke on July 20, the 52nd anniversary of the 1974 military intervention in Cyprus, as Greek City Times reported. Greek authorities are monitoring multiple possible deployment routes, including waters around Cyprus, areas claimed under Turkey's 'Blue Homeland' doctrine, or south of Crete near Libya.

The EU's foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas last week called on Turkey to 'respect the sovereignty and sovereign rights' of the Republic of Cyprus. The Cypriot foreign ministry declared the pipeline agreement 'illegal,' calling it part of efforts to 'consolidate faits accomplis of the occupation.' Israel also reaffirmed its support for Cyprus's sovereignty and opposed unilateral changes to the status quo.
sections.whyItMatters: The seismic survey navtex converts a diplomatic MOU into an operational timeline. If Turkey proceeds with surveys through August, it will test both Greek restraint and EU response at a moment when Ankara needs Western goodwill for defense procurement.

sections.heading: State Department: Turkey Still Short on F-35 Requirements
sections.body:
The US State Department has told Congress that Turkey has not yet met the legal conditions for any potential F-35 delivery, according to a letter from the Office of Legislative Affairs to Democratic Representative Wesley Bell, reported by Protothema.

The letter, sent in response to Bell's inquiry about US-Turkey relations and CAATSA sanctions, states that US policy remains governed by Section 231 of CAATSA and Section 1245 of the FY2020 NDAA. Before any F-35 transfer can proceed, Ankara must: (1) no longer possess the Russian S-400 system or associated equipment, (2) provide assurances it will not acquire the system again, and (3) satisfy remaining certification requirements. The State Department stated plainly that 'these conditions have not yet been met.'

The letter adds that following Trump's recent meeting with Erdogan in Ankara, the US will 'continue working with Turkey to resolve the S-400 issue while also seeking to deepen cooperation within NATO.' On Hamas, it acknowledges continued concerns about Turkey's ties to the group but credits Ankara with helping advance the Gaza ceasefire's first phase.

This comes amid mixed signals: while the State Department letter reinforces legal barriers, Turkish Aerospace CEO confirmed that the US has cleared an export license for KAAN fighter engines, and Baykar's joint venture with Leonardo (LBA Systems) was formally launched at the Farnborough Airshow — suggesting component-level defense cooperation continues even while the headline F-35 question remains stalled.
sections.whyItMatters: The gap between rhetorical warming and statutory reality persists. Turkey can buy engines for its indigenous fighter and form UAV joint ventures, but the F-35 door stays locked until the S-400 is resolved — and the State Department just put that in writing to Congress.

sections.heading: DW Correspondent Freed After 25 Hours, Hit With Travel Ban
sections.body:
Deutsche Welle correspondent Alican Uludag was released Wednesday under judicial supervision after approximately 25 hours in police custody, DW reported. He had been detained Tuesday on new charges of inciting hatred and publicly spreading misleading information — just two months after being released pending trial in a separate case involving insults to President Erdogan.

An Ankara criminal court imposed an international travel ban and ordered Uludag to report to police four times a week, according to DW Turkish and Turkish Minute. He denies all charges.

The German government expressed 'high irritation' over the renewed detention, with a spokesperson telling Reuters that Turkish authorities were acting in violation of press freedom commitments Ankara made by joining the Council of Europe and signing the European Convention on Human Rights. DW Director General Barbara Massing called the re-arrest 'deeply concerning.'

Turkish press organizations gathered outside the Ankara courthouse, with Journalists' Union Ankara branch head Sinan Tartanoglu noting: 'There are many journalists in prison and many under investigation. We want to be able to report the news and express our criticism freely.'
sections.whyItMatters: Uludag's re-detention on new charges while already on conditional release signals escalating pressure on critical journalism. Berlin's 'high irritation' adds a diplomatic dimension — press freedom is now a live issue in Turkey-EU relations at a moment when Ankara seeks defense cooperation from both Washington and European capitals.

sections.heading: CHP Split Deepens: 95 of 135 Lawmakers Back Ozel's New Party
sections.body:
An overwhelming majority of CHP lawmakers — 95 of 135 — have publicly backed Ozgur Ozel's plan to form a new party, according to Bianet. Ozel announced his resignation from the CHP on Tuesday after a court annulled the party congress that brought him to power, reinstating former leader Kemal Kilicdaroglu.

The split marks the culmination of a widening crackdown on the opposition that dates back to October 2024, when Esenyurt mayor Ahmet Ozer was jailed over alleged PKK links. The crisis escalated in March 2025 with the jailing of Istanbul Mayor Ekrem Imamoglu on charges ranging from graft to espionage, which he denies. His university diploma was annulled, making him ineligible for the presidency under Turkish law.

Several CHP mayors have since defected. Aydin Mayor Ozlem Cercioglu joined the AKP in August 2025; Izmir Mayor Cemil Tugay quit the CHP, citing the court annulment. The AKP has gained a net 14 seats in parliament from opposition defections, bringing its total to 277 deputies.

Reuters reports that the annulment rattled markets, pushing the lira lower and forcing the central bank to sell billions in foreign reserves, though conditions stabilized within a day.
sections.whyItMatters: The CHP is now formally fractured, with the majority of its parliamentary caucus following Ozel into uncharted territory. The AKP gains a stronger parliamentary position, while the opposition's challenge to Erdogan fragments into two competing formations ahead of 2028 elections.

sections.heading: US-Saudi Nuclear Pact Drops 'Gold Standard,' Rings Alarm Bells
sections.body:
The Trump administration approved a 30-year civilian nuclear cooperation agreement with Saudi Arabia, submitted to Congress on Wednesday for a 90-session-day review period. The pact, negotiated under Section 123 of the Atomic Energy Act, notably omits the 'gold standard' — a permanent prohibition on uranium enrichment and spent fuel reprocessing — and does not require Saudi Arabia to adopt the IAEA's Additional Protocol for enhanced inspections, according to Al-Monitor and Firstpost.

The agreement allows for a two-year joint study on whether domestic enrichment is commercially justified. If the US objects after the study, Saudi Arabia would be barred from pursuing enrichment independently or with another country for 10 years. The enrichment facility would operate under a 'black box' arrangement with US companies, keeping sensitive technology inaccessible to Saudi personnel. Westinghouse's AP1000 reactor is expected to be a leading technology deployed under the deal.

Criticism was swift. Senator Chris Murphy said the agreement 'will set off a nuclear race in the region, further disincentivizing Iran from limiting its own program.' Israel voiced opposition to a Saudi civil nuclear program. The deal's inconsistency is striking: one of the stated justifications for the US military campaign against Iran was Tehran's refusal to give up enrichment — yet the Saudi deal explicitly permits a pathway to it.

For Turkey, the implications are direct. If Saudi Arabia secures enrichment rights, Ankara will face pressure to explain why its own civil nuclear program (Akkuyu, operated by Russia's Rosatom) operates under tighter constraints, and regional proliferation concerns will compound existing defense calculations.
sections.whyItMatters: The removal of the gold standard creates a double standard that Turkey will not fail to notice. Ankara's leverage arguments in future nuclear and defense negotiations just gained a new data point: Washington is willing to bend proliferation rules for strategic partners.

sections.heading: Houthis Strike Saudi Tankers, Oil Reaches Six-Week High
sections.body:
Yemen's Houthi militia claimed responsibility for attacking two Saudi oil tankers — the Encelia and Layla — in the Red Sea on Wednesday, using ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, and drones. Saudi authorities confirmed that one vessel, the Encelia, caught fire, according to Reuters. The attacks came after the Houthis declared a 'maritime embargo' on Saudi-linked shipping in the Red Sea.

The strikes represent the first Houthi attacks on Saudi vessels since the group announced its blockade. Nearly 10 vessels rerouted following the announcement, and the Houthis warned of deeper strikes on Saudi refineries. The War Zone reported that the group cited the tankers' violation of the ban as justification.

Oil prices have responded accordingly. Brent crude has returned to the mid-$90s per barrel, a six-week high, after briefly dipping near $70 when a ceasefire seemed possible earlier this year, according to Foreign Policy. US gasoline prices are back above $4 per gallon. More critically, global oil stockpiles are falling rapidly, and analysts now expect the Strait of Hormuz to remain disrupted for the remainder of 2026 at minimum, with single-digit tanker transits becoming the norm.

For Turkey, the energy cost pressure is immediate and compounding. The Hormuz disruption and now Red Sea tanker attacks shorten the list of viable oil supply routes, amplifying the strategic value of Turkey's existing pipeline infrastructure (Kirkuk-Ceyhan, BTC) — and of the Cyprus gas pipeline now under survey.
sections.whyItMatters: The Houthi move opens a second front in the oil supply crisis beyond Hormuz. Turkey's geographic position as an energy corridor gains value with every tanker that reroutes — but import costs rise in lockstep.

sections.heading: Baykar-Leonardo Launch LBA Systems UAV Joint Venture
sections.body:
Turkey's Baykar and Italy's Leonardo formally launched LBA Systems, their joint UAV venture, at the Farnborough International Airshow. The company will produce a family of unmanned platforms blending Leonardo's sensor, electronics, and certification expertise with Baykar's drone design and manufacturing capabilities.

The product lineup includes: KALKAN (80kg-class ISR UAV), Bayraktar TB2 (tactical UAV in multiple configurations), Astore Levante (STOL drone for aircraft carriers and small naval vessels), Bayraktar AKINCI (HALE tactical UAV with deep strike capability), and KIZILELMA (indigenous stealth combat drone undergoing advanced testing).

Manufacturing is split between Italy and Turkey: the Astore Levante and KIZILELMA will be produced at Leonardo's Italian facilities, while the TB2 and AKINCI remain in Turkey. The joint venture will pursue NATO-standard certification leveraging Leonardo's experience, positioning it to sell to European and allied defense markets.

The Leonardo CEO separately told Reuters that the deadline for a new country to join the GCAP fighter jet program (the UK-Italy-Japan sixth-generation project) should be set for next year.
sections.whyItMatters: LBA Systems gives Turkey a certified European production pathway for its drone platforms — sidestepping the political barriers that have complicated direct Baykar sales to NATO members. It's also a hedge: if the F-35 door stays shut, UAV cooperation with Leonardo opens a different one.

bottomLine: Turkey moved the Cyprus gas pipeline from diplomatic agreement to operational survey today, deploying the Oruc Reis through August 30 in a step that will test Greek and EU restraint. Washington formally confirmed what Ankara already knew — the F-35 remains locked behind S-400 conditions — even as Turkey deepens defense-industrial ties through the Baykar-Leonardo joint venture and the KAAN engine license. At home, the CHP's parliamentary majority followed Ozgur Ozel into a new party, fracturing the main opposition at a moment when press freedom pressure intensified with DW correspondent Uludag's re-detention and travel ban. The broader energy picture grew more acute: Houthi strikes on Saudi tankers opened a new front beyond Hormuz, oil returned to the mid-$90s, and the US-Saudi nuclear pact dropped the 'gold standard' enrichment prohibition — a double standard Ankara will reference in future negotiations.
sources: Cyprus Mail, Greek City Times, Protothema, Deutsche Welle, Turkish Minute, Bianet, Reuters, Foreign Policy, Al-Monitor, Firstpost, NDTV, The War Zone, Times Now, Devdiscourse, Anadolu Agency, RaillyNews, Breaking Defense, Washington Post, NYT, Spiegel
